title: KV cache eviction, paging, and prefix reuse deep dive - Starlight Analytics
summary: SE-led deep dive into Redwood's KV cache architecture after the customer observed increased eviction rates and paging for long-context sessions. Discussed LRU behaviors, cache sizing, prefix reuse patterns, and potential mitigations (tuning of batching, KV retention, and paging thresholds). Agreed on benchmark repro and follow-up checklist.
next_steps: Redwood: run repro workload with customer's sample prompts and share raw logs (by 2026-04-05)
Starlight: provide representative long-context prompt set and traffic profile (by 2026-04-03)
Redwood: share KV cache internals doc and recommended config snippet (by 2026-04-04)
Schedule follow-up check-in to review benchmark results (tentative 2026-04-08)
SE to open internal ticket for exploring hybrid paging thresholds and improved eviction diagnostics
action_items: Maya Patel: send security and deployment doc links after call (2026-04-02)
Liam Chen: run canonical repro and upload logs to shared drive (2026-04-05)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-01 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~65 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Carlos (VP Eng - Starlight), Anika (ML Platform), Derek (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on the KV cache behavior you reported, and Liam will lead the technical bit.
[00:16] Carlos: Thanks, yeah we've been seeing spikes in token latency and a lot of KV cache evictions when sessions go beyond ~8k tokens, mean throughput drops.
[00:30] Liam: ok, can you describe workload? are these interactive chat sessions with reused prefixes or many unique prefixes?
[00:45] Anika: mostly a few reused prefixes (customer profile + conversation history) but then users paste long transcripts, so sequence length jumps. We suspect prefix reuse but also paging to host memory.
[01:02] Liam: cool. quick overview: our KV cache is an LRU-ish segmented cache that lives on-GPU; when the working set exceeds capacity we either evict least-recently-used kv pages or move cold pages to host (paging) depending on policy and memory pressure. Eviction shows as misses and causes recompute of kv for those tokens.
[01:25] Derek: are those pages compressed or quantized? we use a quantized model (4-bit) in your hosted config.
[01:35] Liam: good question — quantized activations still produce KV structures that are smaller, but there's per-layer overhead. In some cases quantization changes memory alignment and can increase the number of pages, which affects eviction churn. we have seen up to 10-15% difference in KV footprint between per-channel and per-tensor quant profiles.
[02:00] Carlos: the symptom: tail latency spikes and sometimes context resets for certain users, which looks like the system is evicting prefixes then recomputing — causing token timeouts in our app.
[02:15] Liam: that lines up. two axes: 1) eviction policy/thresholds and 2) paging fallback behaviour. paging reduces GPU memory pressure but adds CPU->GPU transfer latency during access. If highly reused prefixes get paged rather than kept, you'll see repeated transfer costs.
[02:40] Anika: what's the default threshold for moving to host vs evict?
[02:46] Liam: default is to prefer paging when on-GPU memory is near capacity but we also have a per-workload hysteresis window. it's tunable per deployment (Dedicated/Private). In hosted we usually set conservative paging to avoid OOM.
[03:05] Maya: also worth noting we have an adaptive prefetch heuristic for prefix reuse; if the system detects a prefix reused > X times in a short window it pins that prefix for longer. but the heuristic can be conservative to protect throughput.
[03:24] Derek: how well does that heuristic work with many long contexts where prefixes are large (several thousand tokens)?
[03:32] Liam: it weakens with large prefixes because pinning large prefixes consumes more of the working set; the heuristic looks at reuse frequency normalized by prefix size. sometimes it underestimates the value of pinning mid-sized prefixes which are frequently reused.
[03:50] Carlos: ok we definitely have mid-size prefixes that are reused across sessions — e.g., user profile + 2-3 prior turns, then the pasted transcript is the long tail.
[04:02] Liam: two immediate mitigations: 1) increase pin window for mid-size prefixes (config change) 2) tune batcher to reduce concurrent unique prefixes per GPU — more batching of similar prefixes keeps reuse higher. both can be done on Dedicated or Private; hosted may require config roll but we can propose changes.
[04:25] Anika: what's the risk to throughput if we increase pinning?
[04:29] Liam: tradeoff is less available cache capacity for new unique requests, so throughput for cold traffic could drop; but with your traffic (high reuse plus long tails) net latency improves. we should simulate with your traffic profile.
[04:48] Maya: we've seen customers benefit from a hybrid policy: pin high-value prefixes, aggressively page truly cold items, and raise prefetch thresholds for known high-reuse paths.
[05:02] Derek: about paging — is it synchronous on access or background prefetch?
[05:08] Liam: both. we have background async prefetch for anticipated reuse (if pattern matches), but first-access of a paged page pays the transfer cost. async prefetch relies on reuse signals; if the reuse pattern is bursty it may miss.
[05:22] Carlos: are there metrics we can surface to see when paging happened vs eviction? our logs just show higher latency.
[05:30] Liam: yes — we can surface "kv_eviction_count", "kv_paged_in_count", and per-prefix heatmap. we'll share a dashboard snippet. in hosted we may need to extend telemetry for your tenant.
[05:46] Anika: would quantization cause more paging frequency?
[05:50] Liam: not directly, but different quant formats change cache footprint and alignment, which can increase page count; also quantization sometimes increases recompute cost which compounds with eviction. we should measure with your exact model/config.
[06:05] Carlos: model is a 70B open model, 4-bit, causal transformer. we run with a top-p decode and 16 beam? (laughter) actually no beams, just sampling. average seq len 3k, 95th percentile 12k.
[06:25] Liam: 12k is substantial. with a 70B model the KV size at 12k can be large; working set will easily exceed a single GPU unless batching/reuse are aggressive.
[06:37] Derek: can we use multi-GPU KV sharding?
[06:40] Liam: yes, we have KV sharding and inter-GPU KV transfer mechanisms. but network hop adds latency; it's best for high throughput streaming scenarios where per-request latency can tolerate the extra hop.
[06:55] Anika: what's your recommended approach for our profile?
[06:58] Liam: initial plan: 1) run repro with your 95th pct prompts and measure eviction vs paging per prefix 2) increase pin window for mid-size prefixes and enable more aggressive async prefetch for those prefixes 3) reduce concurrency per GPU via batching policy to increase reuse ratio 4) test alternative quant profile to see if KV footprint improves (we can try channel-wise quant)
[07:24] Maya: we'll also run a short AB test with and without the increased pinning to measure tail latency and throughput impact.
[07:31] Carlos: what about VPC/on-prem — we might prefer Private for more control? any differences in caching behavior on Private vs Hosted?
[07:40] Liam: behavior is the same runtime, but Private gives you more knobs: you can change paging thresholds, pin windows, and have deeper telemetry with lower friction. Dedicated also allows reserved capacity to avoid cross-tenant eviction churn.
[07:55] Derek: would we get root cause info for evictions on Private?
[07:58] Liam: yes, more detailed KV diagnostics and access to lower-level metrics. we can turn on per-request traces.
[08:08] Anika: can we get an example config snippet for the pin window and paging threshold?
[08:12] Liam: yes I'll share. example: {pin_window_ms: 600000, page_threshold_pct: 88, prefetch_enabled: true, prefetch_window_ms: 300000} — note: this is illustrative; we'll supply tuned numbers after running with your workload.
[08:33] Carlos: any quick wins?
[08:35] Liam: quick wins: reduce max concurrent unique prefixes per GPU (tweak batcher), bump pin window for mid-size prefixes, and turn on additional telemetry to see paged_in counts.
[08:47] Derek: about prefix reuse detection — can we mark some prefixes as sticky from the client side?
[08:52] Liam: yes you can include a prefix_id header in requests; Redwood runtime will treat that as strong reuse signal and pin accordingly. that's probably the fastest win if you can annotate requests.
[09:05] Anika: we can annotate, yes. will that change cost?
[09:09] Liam: not directly, but pinned prefixes consume GPU memory so you might need slightly larger capacity or reserved slots. cost vs latency tradeoff.
[09:18] Carlos: what else should we watch for during the repro run?
[09:21] Liam: watch evictions per prefix, paged_in latencies, and the correlation of long sequences with increased recompute. also track cross-tenant noise if on shared Dedicated.
[09:35] Maya: OK next steps recap: Starlight share prompt set + concurrency, Redwood run repro and share logs + config snippet, then AB test.
[09:45] Carlos: sounds good. any blockers on Redwood side?
[09:48] Liam: none right now; need the prompt set and a short window to run at realistic concurrency.
[09:55] Derek: we'll get that over today.
[10:00] Maya: Great, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the 4/8 check-in. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
